headings.text: 🌳 The route is over budget: what do you try first?

notes.html:
The prompt as a running system. Note 110 draws the layer; 111 is its one shared hop; 112 and 113 are the two budgets every design decision spends; 114 and 115 spend less of them; 116 and 118 say what happens when a call fails; 117, 119 and 120 are short pointers. Read each arrow as a sentence: the cost model is reduced by caching strategy.

Green = CORE, blue = SUPPORTING, yellow = BREADTH. Notes 117 batch, 119 audit and 120 build vs buy share one node.

Reading order:110 reference architecture112 cost model113 latency budget111 gateway114 caching strategy115 routing118 reliability116 degradation117 batch119 audit120 build vs buy

Owners

Ideas several notes touch, and the one note that explains each. The first four rows are owners for the whole pillar.

Idea Owner note

Latency as time to first token plus generation; a stage budget; tail compounding across a chain 113 latency budget
Failure classification; retry multiplication; one deadline; idempotency at the side effect 118 reliability

The choice across cache layers: prefix, exact, semantic 114 caching strategy

What an audit record holds 119 audit

The repair itself: when, how often, with what message parsing and repair loops, not these notes
The prompt-versus-config boundary in general; registry products prompts as code vs config, registries and tooling, not these notes
Gateway duties: credentials, quotas, tenancy LLM application architecture (LLM-Production), not these notes
Routers, cascades and semantic routing as platform design model routing (LLM-Production), not these notes

No merges. Notes 111 and 115 stay SUPPORTING against LLM-Production 12-LLMops, because each keeps a real prompt-shaped half: the binding of prompt to model, and the substitution of prompt tokens for capability. Older text of every note is in 08-Prompt-engineering/_superseded/12-Production Prompt Systems/.

The route is over budget: what do you try first?

  • Trim, cap (112): if the examples you'd cut are what makes it accurate, measure cost per accepted outcome first; a cheaper call that gets rejected costs more.
  • Batch (117): if the data can't leave zero data retention, check first; Anthropic's batches aren't eligible.
  • 💾 Prefix cache (114): if the prefix is below the model's minimum, or traffic is thinner than the lifetime, it writes and never reads.
  • Route (115): if the path is low volume, a second prompt and eval outweigh the saving.
  • Attempt less (116): if the budget is a hard limit for one tenant, make this a rung of the ladder, not a rejection.

This call failed: which response?

  • 🧾 Fail fast (118): spend-cap and quota errors go here, since retrying can't help.
  • Bounded retry (118): if another layer already retries, remove one; attempts multiply.
  • Stop reason (118): a refusal may have an evaluated fallback; a cut-off needs a larger cap or a smaller job.
  • One repair (39): if the repair rate jumped after a release, fix the prompt instead.
  • 🧑 A person, or refuse (118): valid but not allowed is never retried.

The third choice, which cache layer, is the diagram in 114: start with the prefix cache, since it can't return a wrong answer, and make the semantic cache justify itself against the other two.

notes.title: The Prompt Layer Reference Architecture — Six Stages and What Each Arrow Carries
notes.html:
References

Chip Huyen: building a generative AI platform · LiteLLM: life of a request · Langfuse: prompt management · OpenAI: migrate from prompt objects · Anthropic: stop reasons

TL;DR

Between your application and the model sit six stages: template store, renderer, gateway, model, parser, validator. Each owns one question and fails in its own way. The boxes are the easy part. What makes the layer useful is what each arrow carries: the version ID, the usage record, and the mark on untrusted text. A rule in the prompt is a request; a rule in the validator is enforced.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery request
Flow:template version + slotsprompt + version IDmodelparservalidatoryour code acts
validatorone repair, then a safe refusallogged against the version

Recall

Prompt Answer
The six stages? Template store, renderer, gateway, model, parser, validator.
Where is the version ID stamped? At render; every metric and trace joins on it.
Renderer vs gateway? Renderer: what the prompt says. Gateway: which model and how it's called.
Parser vs validator? Parser: is it well-formed? Validator: is it true and permitted?
What survives a model that ignores the prompt? The validator and the permissions behind it.
Draw by hand: the request path Six boxes in order, each arrow labelled with what it carries, plus the failure edge.

The idea

A support product has prompts as f-strings in four services. One morning refunds go wrong. You can't say which prompt version produced the bad answers, because versions don't exist. You can't roll back without a build. Cost per feature is a guess taken from an invoice, and "the model was told not to refund other people's orders" turns out to be the only control.

Nothing was broken in any one place. Rendering, model choice and acceptance were all inside the same function, so none could be observed, replaced or rolled back separately.

Separating them gives each question one home: which version ran, what the model was sent, which model answered, whether the output was well-formed, whether acting on it is allowed. A rendered prompt becomes a pure function of a template version and its slot values, so you can reproduce any past request.

The trade: a shared library, and later a service, in your critical path, in exchange for attribution, one-move rollback and a place to enforce rules. Below a second feature it doesn't pay.

How it works

One request, read top to bottom. Green stages are your code, so they hold whatever must be guaranteed.

Everything above the model is under your control; the model's output is an untrusted proposal until the validator accepts it.

Rule What actually happens
The renderer is the only path to a string It resolves the label, fills slots, marks untrusted text, truncates a designated slot, stamps the version. An f-string skips all five silently.
Check the stop reason before parsing Truncation and refusal arrive as a normal response, so the parser never sees why.
Labels move, versions don't Immutable versions make a trace reproducible; a movable label makes rollback one move.
The store is in the request path Keep the last good version in the client. Langfuse's SDK does this: 60-second default, refreshed in the background.
The platform line is the render boundary Platform owns store, renderer, gateway, framework; products own templates, slots, schemas, eval sets.

Who owns what, and how each stage fails:

Stage Owns Fails as First control
Template store versions, labels wrong version live protected labels
Renderer slots, marking, truncation, stamp untagged requests; the wrong slot cut one code path
Gateway model, retries, budgets total outage; lost attribution its own SLO
Model generation provider incident a pinned ID, an evaluated fallback
Parser text to typed object repairs that hide drift schema enforcement
Validator true, safe, permitted skipped rules in code

Evolution

Lineage:Jul 2024 Chip Huyen's platform build-upAug 2024 schema-enforced output shrinks the parserJun 2026 OpenAI de-emphasises prompt objects30 Nov 2026 v1/prompts scheduled to shut down
  • Maturity: 🟡 Maturing (Oct 2026): the stages are settled; where the store lives is not. Langfuse builds managed versions and labels while OpenAI moves prompts back into code.
  • Stronger-model test: no. A better model reduces parser and repair work; it doesn't tell you which version ran or whether a refund is allowed. What won't change: a model's output is a proposal until code outside it accepts it.
  • Checked on: the OpenAI dates and the Langfuse behaviour were read on 31 Oct 2026.

Code

One code path from template to accepted object, with each stage testable alone.

MODEL_ROUTE = "support.triage"                            # the gateway maps this to a pinned model ID
tpl = store.resolve("support.triage", label=env)          # label → immutable version; rollback moves a label
rendered = renderer.render(tpl,
    slots={"ticket": untrusted(ticket_body), "kb": chunks},   # ① marked here, so it can be wrapped
    budget=WINDOW[MODEL_ROUTE])                               # ② cuts the kb slot, never the instructions
resp = gateway.call(rendered, route=MODEL_ROUTE, schema=Triage,  # ③ version and tenant go on the trace
                    tenant=ctx.tenant)
if resp.stop_reason != "end_turn":                        # ④ cut off or refused: not a parse problem
    return fallback(resp.stop_reason, ctx)
obj = parser.parse(resp, Triage)                          # ⑤ well-formedness only
verdict = validator.check(obj, ctx)                       # ⑥ facts and permissions, from your database
emit(tpl.version, resp.model, resp.usage, verdict.ok)     # every metric joins on the version ID
return obj if verdict.ok else fallback(verdict.reason, ctx)

Break it: the belief that a parsed object is safe to act on.

import json
raw = '{"order_id": "4412", "action": "refund", "amount": 39.0}'  # the model's reply
obj = json.loads(raw)                                  # parser: is it well-formed?
SHAPE = {"order_id": str, "action": str, "amount": float}
shape_ok = all(isinstance(obj[k], t) for k, t in SHAPE.items())
orders_of_user = {"4413", "4419"}                      # from your database, not the prompt
allowed = obj["order_id"] in orders_of_user            # validator: is it permitted?
print(shape_ok, allowed)
# look for: True False
# naive belief predicts: True True, because it parsed

Run on Python 3.15, it prints True False. The reply was perfect in shape and refunds someone else's order, which no schema can catch.

Measure it

  • Offline: contract tests per stage: rendering is byte-stable for a version and its slots, and the validator rejects a golden set of well-formed bad objects, against the previous release.
  • In production: untagged-request rate (target zero), validator rejects per version and rule, direct-to-provider traffic at the network edge. Any untagged request means attribution is already wrong.
  • Enforced by: the code shown: the validator, the gateway and one render path. Prompt instructions about what's allowed are a request only.

Interview

30-second answer: The prompt layer is six stages: a template store, a renderer that stamps the version, a gateway that picks the model and retries, the model, a parser for shape and a validator for truth and permission. The value is in what the arrows carry, especially the version ID, because that's what makes cost, quality and rollback attributable. And the gotcha: parse success isn't correctness.

Q · Mechanism — Why is the renderer a component rather than string formatting at the call site? Three things must happen in exactly one place. Version stamping: only if rendering is the sole path can every request carry its version. Slot discipline: untrusted text is marked here, and the budget cuts a chosen slot. Determinism: the output is a pure function of version and slots, so any past request can be rebuilt. An f-string loses all three with no error.

Q · Trade-off — When is all this the wrong answer? The simpler rung is a versioned string in the repo, a schema and a validator: enough for one feature with engineer-written prompts. A template store earns its place when someone other than an engineer edits prompts, a gateway service when a second team shares provider quota. Before that they add a hop, an on-call and a failure mode. The store question is build vs buy.

Q · Failure — One feature starts leaking raw document text after a platform upgrade. Suspect version skew: products on different renderer versions behave differently. I'd compare renderer versions across products in the traces, then diff that feature's rendered prompt against one from before the upgrade. Fix: treat the renderer as a dependency with staged rollout and its own tests, because one bad truncation change hits every feature at once.

Q · Design — Several AI products share one platform team. Where's the line? A platform owning prompt content becomes a roadmap bottleneck; one owning nothing becomes a library nobody upgrades. So I draw it at the render boundary. One gateway with per-product keys and budgets, one versioned renderer that refuses to emit without a template name and version, a shared validation framework with product schemas, eval harness from the platform, eval sets from products. I watch bypass first, at network egress. The platform side is LLM application architecture.

Pitfalls

  • "Parsing succeeded, so the output is good"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: schema enforcement makes the parser green almost all the time.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: a schema is about shape. A well-typed refund for someone else's order parses cleanly, as Break it shows.
    ↳ Think instead: parser and validator fail differently and are fixed in different places.
  • Not the same: a prompt version vs a model version
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both are called "the version" on a dashboard.
    ↳ Difference: one is your text, the other the provider's weights. A change in either changes behaviour, and only the pair explains an answer.
    ↳ Think instead: log the whole tuple.
  • "The version ID can be added later"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it looks like an observability detail, and nothing fails without it.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: it is the join key. Without it, per-version quality, cost per outcome and rollback decisions can't be computed, and retrofitting touches every call site.
    ↳ Think instead: stamp it from the first request.
  • "The gateway is a thin proxy"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the code is small and does little per request.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: it concentrates credentials, budgets and retries for every feature, so its outage is total and its bypass silently ends attribution.
    ↳ Think instead: thin in code, load-bearing in failure; give it its own SLO.
  • "We told the model not to, so it's handled"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the instruction works in every demo.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: a prompt is a request, and injected text competes with it in one channel.
    ↳ Think instead: business rules live in the validator.
  • Don't build six stages for one prompt.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the diagram looks like what a serious team has.
    ↳ What goes wrong: you run a service, a store and an on-call for routing that always picks one route.
    ↳ Do instead: a prompt file, a schema and a validator; add a stage when a named problem appears.
  • Shelf life: the stages and the proposal-until-accepted rule are durable; products and which side the store sits on are not.

Connections

Path:prompt versioningthe reference architecturethe gatewaycost modellingreliability engineering
  • Owned elsewhere: LLM application architecture (LLM-Production) covers the platform half.
  • Measured by prompt observability: everything joins on the version ID.
  • Builds on parsing and repair loops: the failure edge.
  • Enforced by defence in depth: checks outside the model.
  • Attacked by indirect injection: slots carry untrusted text.
  • Drilled in design the prompt layer.

notes.title: The LLM Gateway — It Routes a Rendered Prompt and Never Writes One
notes.html:
References

LiteLLM: life of a request · LiteLLM: routing · Anthropic: refusals and fallback · Chip Huyen: building a generative AI platform

TL;DR

The gateway is the one hop every model call crosses. Its platform duties (credentials, quotas, retries) are owned by LLM application architecture (LLM-Production). This note keeps the prompt-shaped half: a rendered prompt is bound to a model and a version, so the gateway refuses a request with no version, and moving to another model is a prompt change, not a network change.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery request
Flow:rendered prompt + version IDbudget checkroute to a deploymentprovider formatcall ─other deployment, same promptretrythe route's own promptusage recorded by version

Recall

Prompt Answer
Does the gateway assemble the prompt? No. It would become a second place prompts live.
Retry vs fallback, in prompt terms? Retry resends the same prompt; a fallback needs a prompt for another model.
What must it record per call? Token classes, model ID, latency and the prompt version it received.

The idea

A primary provider has an outage and the gateway fails over. Availability stays green. An hour later parse failures are up, and the team reads it as a prompt regression. It was a failover: the same text went to a model with different defaults, so the format drifted. Nobody had evaluated that prompt on that model, and the logs couldn't separate the two.

The mistake is treating a rendered prompt as portable. It was written and evaluated for one model, and it can carry parameters that another model rejects. Anthropic, as of Oct 2026, returns a 400 for assistant prefill on Claude 4.6 and later, and for forced tool use on Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Fable 5.1.

So the boundary is strict. The renderer owns what the prompt says. The gateway owns which model answers and how the call is made, and it enforces that every request names its version. A route to another model carries its own prompt version and its own eval. All of this is enforced in code: nothing asks the model for anything.

The trade: a new tier on every call, in exchange for one place that enforces the version contract and records usage. A library does most of it until a second team shares your provider quota.

How it works

The two branches differ in what happens to the prompt.

A retry can stay inside the gateway; a fallback has to reach back for a different prompt version.

Rule What actually happens
Translation changes the request A gateway converts to each provider's format, so cache markers, schema parameters and thinking settings don't map one to one. Test each route.
Usage is recorded off the request path LiteLLM logs and updates spend after the response returns, so accounting adds no database write to the call.
Limits sit with the version The gateway applies budgets per tenant, and the version on each record makes spend attributable to a prompt.

Evolution

Lineage:Jul 2024 gateway named as a platform stage2026 providers add their own fallback: Anthropic's fallbacks beta (Jun 2026), for refusals only
  • Maturity: 🟡 Maturing (Oct 2026): the pattern is common; open-source and hosted products still differ in what they do on the path.
  • Stronger-model test: no. It's about ownership and accounting. What won't change: one hop that sees all traffic, and a prompt that belongs to a model.

Code

A route carries prompt and model together, so a fallback can't reuse the wrong text.

ROUTES = {"support.triage": [                       # as of Oct 2026: each entry was evaluated as a pair
    {"model": "claude-haiku-5-5", "prompt": "triage@v17"},
    {"model": "gpt-6-luna",       "prompt": "triage-openai@v4"},
]}

def call(req):
    if not req.template_version:                    # the contract: no version, no call
        metrics.incr("gateway.untagged"); raise Untagged(req.route)
    check_budget(req.tenant)
    for hop in ROUTES[req.route]:                   # model group by model group
        prompt = renderer.render(hop["prompt"], req.slots)   # re-rendered: a prompt belongs to a model
        try:
            resp = provider_call(hop["model"], prompt, deadline=req.deadline)
        except RetriesExhausted:
            continue
        record(resp.usage, resp.model, hop["prompt"], req.tenant)
        return resp
    raise AllRoutesFailed(req.route)

Measure it

  • Offline: each route's prompt and model pair passes the golden set on its own, against the primary route's result, before it can take traffic.
  • In production: untagged requests (target zero), share of traffic per route, parse rate per route, and direct-to-provider traffic at egress. Parse rate moving with route share means an unevaluated route.
  • Enforced by: the code shown: the gateway refuses untagged calls and applies budgets. A bypass is caught only at the network edge.

Interview

30-second answer: The gateway is the hop all model traffic crosses, for credentials, budgets, routing and retries. The prompt-shaped rules are two. It never writes the prompt, because that would split ownership and break version attribution. And a fallback to another model isn't transparent: that model needs its own evaluated prompt. So routes carry prompt and model as a pair.

Q · Mechanism — What's the difference between a retry and a fallback, in prompt terms? A retry moves between deployments of the same model, so the same rendered prompt is still valid and still evaluated. A fallback moves to a different model, whose behaviour and accepted parameters differ. Anthropic's own fallback rule says it plainly: the request must be valid as a direct request to every model named. So a fallback needs its own rendered prompt.

Q · Trade-off — Library or standalone service? The simpler rung is a wrapper library around the provider SDK: no hop, no new on-call, and most of the behaviour. Its failure is version skew, since every service runs its own copy. A service adds what a library can't do: fairness across services, one place to rotate credentials, and central budgets. I'd build it when a second team shares provider quota, and give it a stricter SLO than anything it serves.

Pitfalls

  • "Failover is transparent"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the API shape is the same and the gateway hides the switch.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: a different model is a different system. Format compliance moves, and the incident looks like a prompt regression.
    ↳ Think instead: a route is a model and prompt pair, evaluated together.
  • Don't assemble prompts in the gateway.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it already sees every call, and adding a line there is one deploy.
    ↳ What goes wrong: prompts now live in two places, and the version on the trace no longer describes what was sent.
    ↳ Do instead: keep text in the renderer, and let the gateway choose routes.
  • Not the same: a deployment vs a model group
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both are "another place to send the request".
    ↳ Difference: deployments serve the same model, so behaviour is unchanged. A model group is another model.
    ↳ Think instead: only the second needs an eval, and that's the line between retry and fallback.
  • Don't build a gateway service for one product with one model.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's the architecture every platform diagram shows.
    ↳ What goes wrong: a hop, a failure mode and an on-call rotation for routing that always picks one route.
    ↳ Do instead: a wrapper library that records usage by version, until quota is shared.
  • Shelf life: which parameters a model rejects changes each release; the prompt-belongs-to-a-model rule won't.

Connections

Path:the reference architecturethe gatewaymodel routingdegradation and fallback
  • Owned elsewhere: rate limiting and quota (LLM-Production) covers limits and fairness.
  • Builds on the coupled system: why a prompt doesn't travel between models.
  • Costed in cost modelling: the usage it records.
  • Measured by prompt observability: per-version series.

notes.title: Cost Modelling — Four Token Prices, One Hit Rate and the Right Denominator
notes.html:
References

Anthropic: pricing · OpenAI: pricing · Gemini API: pricing · OpenAI: prompt caching · Chip Huyen: building a generative AI platform

TL;DR

One call has four token prices: fresh input, cache write, cache read and output. The hit rate decides two of those terms and your output length decides a third. Which term is largest depends on the route, so you evaluate the sum instead of assuming. So report cost per accepted outcome, because retries and rejected answers never show in cost per call.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery request
Flow:rendered promptfresh, written, read tokensoutput tokens at k × inputcost of one callaccepted outcomescost per outcome, per version

Recall

Prompt Answer
The four terms of one call? Fresh input, cache write, cache read, output; each with its own multiplier.
The output ratio today? k = 5 on the newest models of all three providers.
Above which hit rate does caching pay? q > (w − 1) / (w − h): about 0.21 at w = 1.25.
The denominator to report? Accepted outcomes, not calls.
Which limit is enforced? max_tokens is; "be brief" is only a request.
Draw by hand: one call's bill Five rows: cold, warm, no cache, hit rate 0.9, hit rate 0.2, in input-token units.

The idea

A team ships a shorter prompt, 10% cheaper per call, and the dashboard shows a win. The prompt also fails the validator more often: acceptance falls from 0.97 to 0.85, so each accepted answer costs about 3% more. Cost per call moved one way and the unit that earns money moved the other.

The second trap: "output is the expensive side", so the team caps a route that returns a 41-token label under a 3,200-token prefix. Output was never that route's largest term.

A cost model fixes both by writing the bill as a sum per route, with every input taken from the usage record.

The trade: a few fields logged per call, in exchange for levers ranked on your traffic instead of on advice. max_tokens and a gateway budget are enforced; a brevity instruction is a request.

How it works

Every price is a multiple of r, the base input price, so the sum survives a price change.

c(call)    = r · ( F + w·W + h·R + k·O )     ← F fresh, W written, R read, O output tokens incl. thinking
E[prefix]  = r · P · ( q·h + (1−q)·w )       ← P prefix tokens, q share of calls that hit
caching wins when  q > (w − 1) / (w − h)     ← below this, the write premium outruns the reads
c(outcome) = spend / accepted = c(call) / p  ← p: share of calls that pass parse and validator
examples   = n · T · (q·h + (1−q)·w) / k     ← n examples of T tokens, priced in output tokens
fine-tune  : N > C / (r·ΔP·m − u)            ← C training, ΔP tokens dropped at multiplier m, u serving uplift

The values of w, h and k are in Numbers and the chapter map's Landscape. Break-even in number of requests is owned by provider prompt caching; the sum above is the same idea per call.

A worked call: prefix P = 3,200, fresh F = 180, output O = 41, with w = 1.25, h = 0.05, k = 5, in units of one input token.

Step Fresh Prefix Output Total
Cold: prefix written 180 4,000 205 4,385
Warm: prefix read 180 160 205 545
No cache at all 180 3,200 205 3,585
Hit rate 0.9 929
Hit rate 0.2 3,617

At a hit rate of 0.2 caching costs slightly more than no cache: hit rate, not the decision to cache, is the engineering problem.

The longer entry needs a much higher hit rate, so buy it only when requests arrive further apart than the short lifetime.

Rule What actually happens
The price can depend on prompt length Haiku 5.5, OpenAI long context and Gemini's Pro models charge a higher rate above a size, for the whole request.
Thinking is output On a model that thinks by default, O is larger than the visible answer.
Usage fields add up differently Anthropic's input_tokens excludes cached tokens; OpenAI's includes them.
Gemini adds a fifth term Explicit cache storage, priced per token-hour.

Evolution

Lineage:Apr 2024 OpenAI batch at half priceAug 2024 Anthropic prices cache writes and reads separatelyOct 2024 Anthropic batch2026 read multipliers below 0.1× on the newest modelsOct 2026 Haiku 5.5 priced by prompt length
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Oct 2026): all three providers publish these token classes; only the multipliers keep moving.
  • Stronger-model test: no. Stronger models only change the inputs: thinking raises O. What won't change: tokens times price, over accepted outcomes.
  • Checked on: every multiplier here was read from the three pricing pages on 31 Oct 2026.

Code

Two functions over the usage record; the rates live in a dated table.

MODEL = "claude-sonnet-5-5"                    # as of Oct 2026
RATE = load_rates(MODEL)                       # r, k, w_5m, w_1h, h: a dated table, reviewed quarterly

def call_cost(u, rate=RATE) -> float:          # Anthropic's fields; OpenAI's input_tokens includes cached
    written = u.cache_creation                 # split by lifetime: the two writes are priced differently
    return rate.r * (u.input_tokens
        + rate.w_5m * written.ephemeral_5m_input_tokens
        + rate.w_1h * written.ephemeral_1h_input_tokens
        + rate.h * u.cache_read_input_tokens
        + rate.k * u.output_tokens)            # thinking is inside output_tokens

def cost_per_outcome(calls) -> float:
    spend = sum(call_cost(c.usage) for c in calls)        # retries and rejects stay in the numerator
    accepted = sum(1 for c in calls if c.parsed and c.valid)
    return spend / max(accepted, 1)                       # zero accepted must page, not divide by zero

Break it: two beliefs: output is always the largest term, and 10% cheaper per call means 10% cheaper.

def call(fresh, read, write, out, w=1.25, h=0.05, k=5):
    return fresh + w * write + h * read + k * out      # in units of one input token
A = call(fresh=180, read=3200, write=0, out=41)        # long stable prefix, short answer
B = call(fresh=180, read=3200, write=0, out=400)       # same prompt, long answer
print(A, B, round(5 * 41 / A, 2), round(5 * 400 / B, 2))  # output's share of the bill
old = (A, 0.97); new = (A * 0.90, 0.85)                # v2 is 10% cheaper per call
print([round(c / p, 1) for c, p in (old, new)])
# look for: output is 38% of A, 85% of B; v2 costs more per outcome
# naive belief predicts: output always dominates; 10% cheaper per call is 10% cheaper

Run on Python 3.15, it prints 545.0 2340.0 0.38 0.85, then [561.9, 577.1]. The cheaper version costs 2.7% more per accepted outcome.

Measure it

  • Offline: replay a week of logged usage through the sum per route, for the new version against the live one on the same golden set. It ships only if acceptance doesn't fall.
  • In production: cost per accepted outcome per version and tenant, calls per outcome, read share and output p95. Flat cost per call with rising calls per outcome means retries.
  • Enforced by: max_tokens and the gateway's budget. The arithmetic enforces nothing, and "keep it short" is a request only.

Interview

30-second answer: A call has four token prices: fresh input, cache writes, cache reads and output. I write the bill as a sum per route, so I can see which term is largest instead of assuming. The hit rate decides the cache terms, and it has a break-even below which caching costs extra. I report cost per accepted outcome, because retries and rejects don't appear in cost per call.

Q · Mechanism — Why does a cached prefix change the decision about few-shot examples? Uncached, n examples of T tokens cost nT at the input rate on every call. Inside a prefix they cost q·h + (1−q)·w of that, so at a high hit rate the question moves from "how many can I afford" to "is my prefix stable". Dividing by k quotes them in output tokens, which a product owner can read.

Q · Trade-off — Why not switch to a cheaper model straight away? The simpler rungs come first: cap output by structure, make the prefix cacheable, batch whatever has no live user. They carry almost no quality risk. A cheaper model changes r by a large factor, but needs an eval per route, its own prompt and a re-check on every upgrade. I climb to it when the sum shows the remaining cost is r itself and the eval says the task survives.

Q · Failure — Cost per call is flat but the bill is growing faster than traffic. Cost per call hides this by construction. I plot calls per outcome, read share, input and output tokens per version. Rising calls per outcome is repair loops or rejects. A falling read share is a changed prefix or requests arriving further apart than the lifetime. Rising input is context creep. Whichever moves names the cause.

Q · Design — Per-seat pricing on a multi-tenant feature: how do you stop one tenant inverting the margin? Revenue is flat per user and cost isn't, so per-tenant cost must be measured and capped. Every call carries tenant, route and version; the gateway records the token classes. A soft budget degrades, a hard one refuses. The shared prefix stays above tenant text. I watch cost per outcome at the top tenant percentile first. The layer is the reference architecture.

Compare

Lever Term it moves Effect Quality risk
Cap output by structure O proportional cut-off answers if capped blindly
Prefix cache W, R the chart above none, but needs a stable prefix
Batch or flex tier every term × 0.5 half none; no live user allowed
Cheaper model r price ratio high; needs an eval per route
Trim input F small once cached can remove the chunk that mattered

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Output ratio k 5 current Anthropic models; OpenAI GPT-6 family; Gemini 4 Argon and 3.8 Flash cited (volatile, as of Oct 2026)
Write multiplier w 1.25, or 2 for Anthropic's 1 hour, 2.5 for OpenAI's 12 hours Anthropic; OpenAI GPT-5.6 and later cited (volatile, as of Oct 2026)
Read multiplier h 0.1 by default; 0.05 and 0.025 on the newest models see the Landscape per model cited (volatile, as of Oct 2026)
Batch and flex × 0.5 all three providers; Anthropic has batch only cited (volatile, as of Oct 2026)
Hit-rate break-even 0.21 at w = 1.25; 0.51 at w = 2; 0.61 at w = 2.5 (w − 1) / (w − h), h = 0.05 derived

Pitfalls

  • "Output is always the biggest line"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: output is priced five times input, and the advice is repeated everywhere.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: a label under a long prefix is mostly input: 38% output in Break it, less still without the cache.
    ↳ Think instead: evaluate the sum per route, then cut the largest term.
  • "Cost per call is the unit economic"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's on the provider's dashboard and it falls when you trim.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: retries and rejected answers sit outside it, so a cheaper prompt that fails more looks like a win while costing more per answer.
    ↳ Think instead: accepted outcomes are the denominator, and a prompt change is priced with its acceptance rate.
  • Not the same: max_tokens vs "be brief"
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both are described as output-length control.
    ↳ Difference: max_tokens is enforced and cuts generation off, possibly mid-sentence. "Be brief" is a request that shortens the typical answer but guarantees nothing.
    ↳ Think instead: shape length with the output contract; keep the cap as the fuse.
  • "Tokens are tokens across providers"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the usage objects look alike, so one parser seems enough.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: Anthropic's input_tokens excludes cached tokens and OpenAI's includes them. Reuse one formula and you bill cached tokens twice or lose them.
    ↳ Think instead: one adapter per provider, tested against an invoice.
  • "We saved 85% with caching"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: a warm call against a cold call shows a huge drop.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the cold call carries the write premium, so it's the wrong baseline. Compare against no cache at the real hit rate.
    ↳ Think instead: state the baseline with every saving.
  • Don't build a cost platform for a route with no traffic.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the model is elegant and the demo is impressive.
    ↳ What goes wrong: a router and per-tenant budgets on low volume add evals and failure modes that outweigh the saving.
    ↳ Do instead: cap output, order the prefix, batch what can wait, and revisit when the sum shows a term worth attacking.
  • Shelf life: the sum is permanent. Every multiplier moved in the past year, so re-read the Landscape before quoting one.

Connections

  • Builds on window budgeting: it decides F and R before anything is priced.
  • Used by caching strategy: the sum says which layer pays.
  • Measured by prompt observability: token classes and acceptance per version.
  • Owned elsewhere: cost optimization (LLM-Production) covers platform spend and committed pricing.
  • Enforced by the gateway: budgets per tenant.
  • Drilled in cost-model a million calls.

notes.title: Latency Budget — Time to First Token Plus Generation, and Where Each Millisecond Goes
notes.html:
References

Anthropic: reducing latency · OpenAI: latency optimization · Anthropic: prompt caching · Anthropic: thinking · Chip Huyen: building a generative AI platform

TL;DR

A call's latency is time to first token plus generation. Your prompt mostly moves the first term and your output length moves the second, so the two have different fixes and need separate alarms. Streaming shortens neither; it changes what the user waits for. Each step of a chain adds a full round trip, and its tail adds too: budgets set per step at p95 don't add up to a p95 for the chain.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery request
Flow:requestprovider queue ─cached prefix read, fresh tokens processedthinking, if anyfirst visible token ─one output token at a timelast tokenusable answer

Recall

Prompt Answer
The latency sum? TTFT + (output tokens − 1) × time per output token.
What does a cache read shorten? Time to first token; generation is unchanged.
What does streaming change? When the user sees text; not when the answer ends.
Why does a serial chain hurt the tail? Any slow step makes the whole run slow; the chances compound.
What is hidden thinking on this sum? Output tokens that arrive before the first visible text.
Draw by hand: the timeline Queue, input processing, first token, generation, last token, validation; mark what streaming and caching touch.

The idea

A chat feature feels slow, so a team cuts the system prompt in half. Nothing changes that a user can feel. The answers are long, and OpenAI's guide (as of Oct 2026) says cutting 50% of a prompt "may only result in a 1–5% latency improvement", while cutting 50% of output "may cut ~50%". Those figures are the vendor's and are task-dependent, yet the shape holds: output tokens are produced one at a time, while the prompt is read in one pass.

The reverse failure also exists. A team sends a long contract with every question and the first token takes seconds. Here input processing is the problem, and a cached prefix fixes it without trimming anything.

So one number for "LLM latency" can't guide either fix. Splitting it tells you which term to attack, and turns an interactive budget into a list of what fits.

The trade: a budget per stage costs you measurement on every call and rules out designs early, including chains and reasoning you would have liked to keep.

How it works

The definitions of TTFT and time per output token are owned by latency metrics (LLM-Production). The sum, as a function of your prompt:

TTFT      = t_net + t_queue + t_read(C) + t_in(F)      ← C cached prefix, F fresh tokens: t_read(C) << t_in(C)
visible   = TTFT + H · g                               ← H hidden thinking tokens, g time per output token
total     = TTFT + (O − 1) · g                         ← O output tokens, thinking included
usable    = total + t_parse + t_validate               ← structured output is usable only when complete
serial    = Σ total_i                                  ← each step pays its own network, queue and input
parallel  = max_i total_i                              ← the slowest branch

One call on a timeline, with what each lever touches.

Two different things can break this path, so a stage budget needs a first-token alarm and an end-to-end one.

Rule What actually happens
Serving papers call input processing "prefill" It's unrelated to assistant prefill; this pillar says input processing.
Hidden thinking delays visible text Anthropic: display: "omitted" starts text sooner; you still pay for the tokens, and lowering effort is what cuts them.
Streaming and validation conflict You show text before the validator has seen it; structured output is only usable at the end.
Cold compiles land on the request path A new schema's first request can pay a compile; see constrained decoding.

Evolution

Lineage:Aug 2024 Anthropic's prompt cache makes input processing skippableOct 2024 OpenAI automatic caching2026 thinking on by default, and an effort setting as a speed controlJul 2026 OpenAI renames priority processing "Fast mode"
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Oct 2026): both vendors publish latency guidance built on the same terms.
  • Stronger-model test: no. Reasoning models made it harder, since thinking sits before the first visible token, and paid fast tiers let you buy time. What won't change: output is generated token by token, and serial calls add.
  • Checked on: the vendor sentences and the thinking behaviour were read on 31 Oct 2026; no throughput is quoted, because it varies with model, load and date. Measure yours.

Code

Measure the two terms separately, per version, and put the cap and the deadline in the call.

MODEL = "claude-haiku-5-5"                      # as of Oct 2026; effort is its speed control
async def turn(ctx, deadline_s=2.0):
    t0, first = time.monotonic(), None
    async with asyncio.timeout(deadline_s):     # the budget bounds the whole call, retries included
        async with client.messages.stream(
            model=MODEL, max_tokens=300,        # O is the term you own: the cap bounds the tail
            system=PREFIX, messages=ctx.turn,   # stable prefix first: cache reads shorten TTFT
            output_config={"effort": "low"},    # fewer thinking tokens before the first text
        ) as stream:
            async for text in stream.text_stream:
                first = first or time.monotonic()     # visible first token, not the first event
                ctx.ui.send(text)
            final = await stream.get_final_message()
    metrics.observe("ttft_s", first - t0, tags={"cfg": ctx.cfg})
    metrics.observe("total_s", time.monotonic() - t0, tags={"cfg": ctx.cfg})
    metrics.observe("out_tokens", final.usage.output_tokens, tags={"cfg": ctx.cfg})

Break it: the belief that steps budgeted at 200 ms each make a chain that meets 600 ms at p95.

import random
random.seed(7)
step = lambda: 2000 if random.random() < 0.04 else 200   # ms: a scripted step, 4% slow
one = sorted(step() for _ in range(100_000))
chain = sorted(step() + step() + step() for _ in range(100_000))
p = lambda xs, q: xs[int(q * len(xs))]
print(p(one, .95), 3 * p(one, .95), p(chain, .95), sum(c > 600 for c in chain) / len(chain))
# look for: step p95 200, sum 600, chain p95 2400, 12% of chains over 600 ms
# naive belief predicts: the chain's p95 is the sum of the steps' budgets

Run on Python 3.15, it prints 200 600 2400 0.11511. The step timings are scripted, not measured; the arithmetic is 1 − 0.96³. Every step meets its p95 and the chain misses by four times.

Measure it

  • Offline: replay a set of prompts with and without the change against the current version, and compare p50 and p95 of TTFT and total. Comparing means alone hides what the change did to the tail.
  • In production: p95 first visible token and p95 total per version, plus output tokens p95 and read share. Tail latency that tracks output tokens is yours; tail latency with flat tokens is the queue.
  • Enforced by: max_tokens, the deadline and the gateway timeout. "Answer quickly" is a request only.

Interview

30-second answer: I split latency into time to first token and generation. The prompt mostly affects the first, output length the second. A cached prefix shortens the first, a cap bounds the second, and streaming changes neither but changes what the user waits for. Serial chains pay every term again and compound their tails, so I set a budget per stage and alarm on first token separately.

Q · Mechanism — Why does halving a prompt often do less than halving the output? The model reads the prompt in one pass but generates output one token at a time, so each output token is a separate forward pass. OpenAI's guide gives 1–5% against about 50% for the same cut, on its own example. The exception is a very long uncached prompt, where input processing can dominate first token; there a cached prefix is the fix, since it keeps the context.

Q · Trade-off — One call or a chain of focused calls? The simpler rung is one call with an enumerated output. Each extra hop pays a full round trip and re-reads the previous step's output, and the tail compounds, as Break it shows. I decompose when steps are truly parallel, need different models, or quality collapses in one call, and I need an eval showing that gap. The full decision is prompt chaining.

Q · Failure — p50 is fine, p99 is four times worse. Where do you look? Correlate p99 with output tokens first; a long-output tail explains most of them and a cap fixes it. Then split by cache hit: bursty traffic that outlives the lifetime makes cold calls the tail. Only then blame the provider queue, which shows as variance with flat token counts, and calls for a timeout plus an evaluated fallback.

Q · Design — Budget an interactive voice turn at 1.5 seconds from end of speech to first audio. This is a perceptual deadline, so I design against p95. Only time to first token sits on the critical path, because speech starts on the first sentence boundary and generation overlaps playback. So: cached prefix, a fast model at low effort, no second model call in the turn, and retrieval started on the partial transcript. I watch p95 first token against its slice. The stage budget and measured numbers are in the voice pillar.

Compare

Choice First token Total Worth it when
Longer prompt, uncached grows grows, once the context improves answers
Longer prompt, cached barely moves barely moves the prefix is stable
Reasoning on delays visible text grows with thinking accuracy beats the wait
Serial chain pays per step sum of steps quality collapses otherwise
Parallel calls one hop slowest branch sub-tasks are independent
Streaming unchanged unchanged any text surface

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Cut 50% of a prompt "may only result in a 1–5% latency improvement" the vendor's own framing, not a benchmark cited (volatile, as of Oct 2026): OpenAI guide
Cut 50% of output "may cut ~50% of your latency" same page cited (volatile, as of Oct 2026): OpenAI guide
Chain over 600 ms 11.5% three steps, each 4% slow derived and simulated
Chance a chain has a slow step 1 − (1 − s)^n n steps, each slow with chance s derived

Pitfalls

  • "Shorter prompts make responses faster"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: less text to read sounds like less time.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: it helps only the first-token term, and little of total time on a long answer. A cut can also lose the context the answer needed.
    ↳ Think instead: attack output first, then cache the prefix, and trim last.
  • Not the same: streaming vs faster
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: the product feels faster the moment you enable it.
    ↳ Difference: streaming moves when the user first sees text. Generation time is unchanged, and validators still run at the end.
    ↳ Think instead: report first visible token and total as two numbers; perceived latency isn't throughput.
  • "Mean latency tells me whether we meet the budget"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's the number the provider dashboard leads with.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: a deadline fails on the tail, and tails compound along a chain: 12% over budget in Break it with every step on target.
    ↳ Think instead: budget the whole path at p95, and simulate the chain.
  • Not the same: input processing vs assistant prefill
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: serving material calls prompt processing "prefill", and prompting material uses the word for priming a reply.
    ↳ Difference: one is a compute phase before the first token; the other is text you place in the assistant turn, now rejected by Claude 4.6 and later.
    ↳ Think instead: say input processing, and keep prefill for the turn.
  • "A hidden chain of thought costs no latency"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: nothing appears on screen, and the first event may arrive quickly.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: hidden thinking is still generated, so it delays the first useful text, and it counts as output.
    ↳ Think instead: measure the first visible token, and control thinking with effort.
  • Don't tune latency on a path with no user waiting.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: faster looks better on every dashboard.
    ↳ What goes wrong: you spend effort and quality on nightly jobs nobody is watching.
    ↳ Do instead: for interactive text, stream and cap output first. Move everything else to batch.
  • Shelf life: the sum is permanent; fast tiers, thinking controls and the vendor sentences aren't.

Connections

Path:cost modellinglatency budgetreliability engineering
  • Owned elsewhere: latency metrics (LLM-Production) defines the metrics and their percentiles.
  • Builds on provider prompt caching: the largest first-token lever.
  • Measured by prompt observability: both terms, per version.
  • Used by prompt chaining: each step's round trip.
  • Contrasts with batch: the path where latency stops being a constraint.
  • Drilled in one prompt or a chain.

notes.title: Caching Strategy — Choosing Between a Cheaper Call and No Call
notes.html:
References

Chip Huyen: building a generative AI platform · GPTCache · Anthropic: prompt caching

TL;DR

Three caches get called "the cache". The prefix cache makes the call cheaper and still generates. An exact result cache skips the call for an identical request. A semantic cache skips the call for a similar request, and it is the only one that can return an answer to a different question. So the choice is a correctness decision first and a saving second. Break-even belongs to provider prompt caching, prefix stability to context ordering.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery request
Flow:rendered prompt + scopestored answer

miss ─similar, same scope, same entities─▶ stored answer

missprovidercheaper callfresh answerwritten back by version

Recall

Prompt Answer
The three layers? Prefix cache, exact result cache, semantic cache.
Which can be wrong rather than stale? Only semantic: it matches a different question.
What must every result-cache key hold? Prompt version, model, parameters and tenant scope.

The idea

A support assistant adds a semantic cache and hit rate looks excellent. Then a customer asks about order 4413 and gets the answer stored for order 4412: fluent, plausible, and about someone else's order. Nothing in parsing or validation fires, because the stored answer was valid when it was written.

A prefix cache at a zero hit rate wastes a write premium, and an exact cache at zero does nothing. A semantic cache degrades to a confident wrong answer, because the tokens that decide the answer (a negation, an ID, a date) are the ones similarity compresses away.

So choose by what each layer can get wrong, and make the third justify itself against the first two.

The trade: a result cache removes the call and its cost, and takes on staleness and, for semantic matching, wrong answers. The prefix cache keeps the call and carries neither risk. Scope keys and entity guards are enforced by your code; no part of this is a request to the model.

How it works

Each layer sees only what the one before it missed, so order is part of the design.

The red leaf is the only outcome that can hurt a user without any error being raised.

Rule What actually happens
The key is the contract Leave out prompt version and rollout metrics are meaningless; leave out tenant and a result cache leaks data across tenants.
Invalidation differs by layer Prefix: lifetime, provider-managed. Exact: version or model change. Semantic: those, plus any change to the content it answered from.
Live state never goes in A balance or a status from minutes ago is a wrong answer now.

Evolution

Lineage:2024 exact, semantic and prompt caches listed as one platform stage2026 automatic provider caching makes the prefix layer the default
  • Maturity: 🟡 Maturing (Oct 2026): prefix and exact caching are routine; semantic caching remains a per-domain bet with few maintained defaults. GPTCache's README says it no longer adds support for new APIs or models.
  • Stronger-model test: no. Better models don't change that two similar questions can have different answers. What won't change: a stored answer can only be as right as its key.

Code

Break it: the belief that high similarity means the same question.

import math, re
from collections import Counter
vec = lambda s: Counter(re.findall(r"\w+", s.lower()))    # a toy embedding: word counts
def cos(a, b):
    dot = sum(a[w] * b[w] for w in a)
    return dot / math.sqrt(sum(v * v for v in a.values()) * sum(v * v for v in b.values()))
cached, new = "can I cancel order 4412 today", "can I cancel order 4413 today"
sim = cos(vec(cached), vec(new))
ids = lambda s: set(re.findall(r"\d{3,}", s))
print(round(sim, 3), sim >= 0.8, ids(cached) == ids(new))
# look for: 0.833 True False, a hit for a different order; the guard catches it
# naive belief predicts: high similarity means the same question

Run on Python 3.15, it prints 0.833 True False. The vector is a toy; a real embedding gives a different score, and the guard doesn't depend on that score.

Measure it

  • Offline: on labelled query pairs (same answer, different answer), measure false hits at each threshold, against no semantic cache. Choose the threshold from false hits, not from hit rate.
  • In production: hit rate per layer, sampled false-hit review, and read share per config. Serving an answer from an earlier prompt version means the key is missing it.
  • Enforced by: the key, the scope check and the entity guard, in your code. Provider-side matching and expiry are enforced by the provider.

Interview

30-second answer: There are three caches. The provider's prefix cache makes a stable prefix cheaper and still generates. An exact result cache returns a stored answer for an identical request. A semantic cache matches on similarity, so it can answer a different question. I turn on the first two where they fit, and a semantic cache needs a scope key, an entity guard and a threshold set from labelled pairs.

Q · Mechanism — Why does a semantic cache fail silently? It returns a previously valid answer, so parsing and validation pass. Two questions can sit close in embedding space and have different correct answers, because a single entity, number or negation changes the answer while barely moving the vector. Nothing in the pipeline compared them. So a guard outside the similarity score has to compare the deciding tokens.

Q · Trade-off — Would you put a semantic cache in front of a customer-facing assistant? The simpler rungs are the prefix cache and an exact cache, which carry no correctness risk. I'd add semantic only on static FAQ content, keyed by tenant and locale, with a threshold from labelled pairs and an entity guard. Not on anything personal or live: the scope key would have to be so narrow that hit rate collapses. It has to beat what the first two already save.

Compare

Layer Keyed on Saves Can be wrong?
Prefix cache identical leading tokens input cost, first-token time no
Exact result cache prompt, version, model, parameters, scope the whole call stale only
Semantic cache similarity plus scope the whole call yes
Precomputed answers a known input set the whole call and tail latency stale only

Pitfalls

  • "Caching can't hurt: worst case it doesn't help"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: in most systems a cache miss is just the slow path.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: a prefix cache that never hits pays a write premium on every call, and a semantic cache degrades into wrong answers.
    ↳ Think instead: two of the three layers have a real downside; say which you accepted.
  • Not the same: a prompt cache vs a response cache
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both are "LLM caching" and both reduce the bill.
    ↳ Difference: a prompt cache reuses work on your input and generates fresh. A response cache returns stored text with no call.
    ↳ Think instead: one changes a price, the other changes what the user reads.
  • Don't leave prompt version out of the key.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: a hash of the text seems sufficient, and the hit rate is higher.
    ↳ What goes wrong: answers from the previous version keep serving after a rollout, so your rollout metrics describe the old prompt.
    ↳ Do instead: put version, model and scope in the key, so a release starts clean.
  • Don't add a semantic cache before measuring repetition.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: a vector store and a threshold look like a cheap win.
    ↳ What goes wrong: you take on a correctness risk where exact caching and the prefix cache would have delivered most of the saving.
    ↳ Do instead: log how many requests repeat exactly or nearly, then decide.
  • Shelf life: cache prices and modes move every few months; "key decides correctness" does not.
