notes.title: Model Routing by Difficulty — A Rich Prompt on a Small Model Against a Thin One on a Big Model
notes.html:
References

Ong et al. 2024: RouteLLM · LiteLLM: routing · Anthropic: pricing · Chip Huyen: building a generative AI platform

TL;DR

Routing sends easy requests to a cheap model and hard ones to an expensive model. Router against cascade, and how learned routers work, are owned by model routing (LLM-Production). The prompt-shaped half: prompt tokens and model capability are partly substitutes, so each route is its own prompt with its own eval. The silent failure is under-routing, a hard request answered plausibly by the small model.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery request
Flow:requestdifficulty scoresmall model, rich cached promptanswer
score high, or validator rejectsbig model, its own promptanswerthreshold review

Recall

Prompt Answer
What is being traded? Prompt investment against model capability, on structured tasks only.
The expensive mistake? Under-routing: wrong, plausible and silent. Over-routing only costs money.
What does a second route cost? A second prompt, a second eval suite and a re-check on every upgrade.

The idea

A team moves ticket classification to a small model with the same short prompt, accuracy falls, and they conclude the small model can't do it. They changed one half of a pair: a small model usually needs examples and an explicit output contract, and that prompt can be far longer before it costs more.

A rich prompt supplies format, examples and constraints, not the ability to hold a long chain of inferences. So the substitution works for extraction and classification, and stops where the difficulty is reasoning depth.

The first decision is empirical. Run a sample through both models and label where the big model won. If it wins everywhere or nowhere, ship one model. Routing pays only when the gap is concentrated in a minority you can identify.

The trade: a lower average price per call, for a second prompt to keep, a second eval to run, and a failure that nothing downstream reports.

How it works

How long may the rich prompt be before it stops saving money? On input alone:

small cheaper when  P_rich · r_small < P_thin · r_big   ← P prompt tokens, r input price
so                  P_rich / P_thin  < r_big / r_small  ← the price ratio is the prompt budget
with a router       c_r < (1 − f)·(c_big − c_small)     ← c_r router cost per call, f share sent to big
with a cascade      cost = c_small + f·c_big            ← the small call is paid on escalation too

The dated ratio is in Numbers; caching widens it. Cost per call is owned by cost modelling.

Rule What actually happens
A route is a pair Different examples, output contract and eval, not the big model's prompt with more words.
Set the threshold on quality Cost is the easy target and quality degrades silently, so bias towards escalation.
A cascade needs a real reject signal A validator can reject. A model's own confidence is weakest on the cases it gets wrong.
Watch the price edges Haiku 5.5 costs five times more per token above 100,000 prompt tokens.

Evolution

Lineage:Jun 2024 RouteLLM: routers trained on preference dataJul 2024 router named as a platform stageOct 2026 small models reach a 40× price gap on Anthropic's line
  • Maturity: 🟡 Maturing (Oct 2026): static routing is common; learned routers depend on data that matches your traffic.
  • Stronger-model test: partly. Stronger small models shrink the hard minority, so a route can disappear. What won't change: two models mean two prompts to keep and evaluate.
  • Checked on: RouteLLM routed between GPT-4 and Mixtral-8x7B (ICLR 2025). Prices were read on 31 Oct 2026.

Code

The route table is data, and a route can't exist without its eval.

ROUTES = {                          # model IDs as of Oct 2026; a route is a tested pair
    "small": {"model": "claude-haiku-5-5", "prompt": "extract-rich@v9", "eval": "run-2231"},
    "big":   {"model": "claude-opus-5-5",  "prompt": "extract-thin@v3", "eval": "run-2231"},
}
def hard(req) -> bool:              # a cheap signal, chosen from your own labelled sample
    return req.n_docs > 2 or req.has_conditions or req.retrieval_top_score < THRESHOLD

def answer(req):
    route = ROUTES["big" if hard(req) else "small"]
    obj = run(route, req)
    if route is ROUTES["small"] and not validator.check(obj, req).ok:   # the escalation signal
        metrics.incr("route.escalated", tags={"v": route["prompt"]})
        return run(ROUTES["big"], req)                                  # the small call stays on the bill
    return obj

Measure it

  • Offline: quality per route on a stratified golden set, against always using the big model. A route ships only if the hard cohort doesn't fall.
  • In production: share per route, escalation rate, sampled review of small-route answers. A falling escalation rate can mean a broken signal, not an easier mix.
  • Enforced by: the router and validator in your code. Beyond what the validator sees, only sampling catches under-routing.

Interview

30-second answer: Routing sends each request to the cheapest model that can handle it. Prompt tokens and capability are partly substitutes: a rich cached prompt can bring a small model close on structured work, not on deep reasoning. Every route is a model and prompt pair with its own eval. The failure to fear is under-routing, because it's silent.

Q · Mechanism — Why can a much longer prompt on a small model still be cheaper? Input cost is tokens times price, so the prompt can grow by the price ratio before input cost matches. On Anthropic's line that's 40× between Opus 5.5 and Haiku 5.5, as of Oct 2026, and caching a stable prefix widens the gap.

Q · Trade-off — Cheap model with a rich prompt, or an expensive model with a thin one? The simpler rung is one model for everything, and I'd stay there unless the sample shows a gap concentrated in a minority. Then a rich prompt on a small model takes high-volume structured work, and the frontier model takes the open-ended minority.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Price ratio 40× on input and on output Opus 5.5 ($4/$20) against Haiku 5.5 ($0.10/$0.50) up to 100,000 prompt tokens cited (volatile, as of Oct 2026)
Router saving "over 2x cost savings" public benchmarks, GPT-4 and Mixtral-8x7B cited (paper)
Trained on someone else's data at the level of a random router RouteLLM on MMLU with Arena data alone, before adding about 1,500 golden samples cited (paper)

Pitfalls

  • "Routing is a cost optimisation, so the risk is spending too much"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the project is justified on the bill, and over-routing shows up there.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: under-routing gives a fluent wrong answer that parses and ships, so the costly failure is invisible.
    ↳ Think instead: bias towards escalation, and sample the small route.
  • "The small model failed, so it can't do this task"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the same prompt looks like a fair comparison.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the prompt was tuned to the big model. Examples and a contract often close the gap on structured work.
    ↳ Think instead: compare pairs, each prompt tuned to its model.
  • "A published router will work on my traffic"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the paper reports strong savings.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: RouteLLM's routers trained on Arena data alone performed like random on MMLU; a small labelled set fixed it.
    ↳ Think instead: label a sample of your own traffic first.
  • Don't route a low-volume path.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the price ratio makes the saving look large.
    ↳ What goes wrong: a second prompt, eval suite and upgrade check outweigh a small absolute saving.
    ↳ Do instead: pick one model, and revisit when the sum shows a real amount.
  • Not the same: routing vs fallback
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both send a request to another model through the same gateway.
    ↳ Difference: routing is chosen by difficulty before the call; fallback is forced by a failure.
    ↳ Think instead: routing is a cost and quality decision; fallback is availability.
  • Shelf life: price ratios change every few months; the pair and its eval don't.

Connections

Path:the gatewaymodel routingcost modelling
  • Owned elsewhere: model routing (LLM-Production) covers routers, cascades and semantic routing.
  • Builds on model-family differences: why each model gets its own prompt.
  • Measured by golden datasets: the hard cohort.
  • Drilled in big model or small model.

notes.title: Degradation & Fallback — Make the Absence Visible to the Prompt
notes.html:
References

Google SRE: addressing cascading failures · Google SRE: handling overload · Anthropic: refusals and fallback · LiteLLM: reliability

TL;DR

Degradation reduces what you attempt; fallback changes who serves it. Circuit breakers and load shedding are platform work, owned by failure modes and resilience (LLM-Production). The prompt-shaped half: when a source fails, the rendered prompt has to say so. An empty slot looks exactly like "nothing matched", so the model answers from nothing and users read it as sourced.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery request
Flow:gather sourcesrender an explicit "unavailable" markerstanding rule in the cached prefixmodel says what it lacksvalidator rejects invented citationsresponse flagged degraded

Recall

Prompt Answer
Degradation vs fallback? Degradation attempts less; fallback changes the model serving it.
What must the prompt know? That a source is missing, as a marker, never an empty slot.
The degraded path's two properties? Cheaper than normal, and exercised before you need it.

The idea

Retrieval times out during a document assistant's busiest hour. The renderer fills <context> with nothing and the call goes ahead. The model answers from what it learned in training, confidently, and users read every answer in this product as sourced. An availability failure has become a fabrication, and every dashboard is green.

The fix starts in the renderer. It distinguishes "searched and found nothing" from "couldn't search" and writes the second as a marker. A standing rule in the cached prefix says what to do on that marker, so the rule is always present and costs nothing extra at failure time. The response carries a degraded flag, so the UI can show it and your metrics can keep the two products apart.

The marker and the rule are a request; the model may still answer. What's enforced sits around it: the renderer writes the marker, and the validator rejects a citation when context was unavailable.

The trade: a marker, a rule and a flag on every route, for a worse answer that is honest about being worse.

How it works

Every failure edge leads somewhere explicit.

No path turns a missing input into an empty string, and no path ends in an unevaluated model.

Rule What actually happens
Spend the ladder in order Drop optional context ─▶ shorten output ─▶ a cheaper model ─▶ a stored or templated answer ─▶ refuse honestly. Each rung costs less than the one above.
A refusal isn't an error On Anthropic it's a normal response with stop_reason: "refusal", so error-based fallback never fires.
Provider fallback has a narrow trigger Anthropic's fallbacks (beta) acts only on a safety classifier decline; rate limits, overload and server errors come back to you.
Different failures, different routes LiteLLM separates fallbacks, content_policy_fallbacks and context_window_fallbacks.

Evolution

Lineage:2016 degraded responses and load shedding in the SRE bookJun 2026 Anthropic's fallbacks betaJul 2026 a "default" mode that picks the fallback per refusal category
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Oct 2026) as a practice; provider-side fallback is still in beta.
  • Stronger-model test: no. A better model still can't tell an outage from an empty result unless you tell it. What won't change: the prompt only knows what you render into it.
  • Checked on: the marker rule is a request whose success depends on the model and is unmeasured here. Test it on your own failure cases.

Code

Break it: the belief that the model can tell "nothing matched" from "search was down".

TPL = "<context{attrs}>{body}</context>\nQuestion: {q}"
def render(q, chunks):
    if chunks is None:                                 # retrieval failed: say so
        return TPL.format(attrs=' status="unavailable"', body="", q=q)
    return TPL.format(attrs="", body="\n".join(chunks), q=q)
naive = TPL.format(attrs="", body="\n".join([]), q="Refund window?")
print(naive.splitlines()[0]); print(render("Refund window?", []).splitlines()[0])
print(render("Refund window?", None).splitlines()[0])
# look for: the first two lines are identical; only the third differs
# naive belief predicts: the model can tell "nothing matched" from "search was down"

Run on Python 3.15, it prints <context></context> twice, then <context status="unavailable"></context>. Without the marker, the two states reach the model as the same bytes.

Measure it

  • Offline: a failure cohort in the golden set (each source removed in turn): rate of honest "unavailable" answers against the unmarked prompt, plus the fallback pair's score against the primary's.
  • In production: degraded share per route, time on fallback, rejected citations while context was unavailable. A green availability chart with rising degraded share is the incident.
  • Enforced by: the renderer's marker, the validator's citation check and the degraded flag. The model obeying the unavailable rule is a request only.

Interview

30-second answer: When a source fails, the worst outcome is an empty slot, because the model answers anyway and users trust it. So the renderer writes an explicit unavailable marker, a standing rule says what to do, and the response is flagged degraded. Model fallback needs its own evaluated prompt. And the degraded path must be cheaper than normal, or it fails when you need it.

Q · Mechanism — Retrieval timed out. What does the prompt look like now? Not the same prompt with an empty block. The renderer emits <context status="unavailable" reason="timeout"/>, and the system prompt already says: if context is unavailable, say so and never present a claim as sourced. That rule sits in the cached prefix, so it's always there. The validator rejects any citation on that request, because the rule alone is a request.

Q · Trade-off — Fall back to another model, or degrade and tell the user? The simpler rung is degrading honestly on the same model. I'd add a fallback route only with an eval run and a dashboard slice, because an unevaluated model trades a visible outage for an invisible quality incident. And it depends what failed: an outage is what fallback is for, but in a brownout, failing over adds load, so I'd shed low-priority traffic first.

Compare

Failure Wrong response Right response
Retrieval timeout empty slot marker, flag, honest answer
Tool error error text inlined as context typed failure; suppress the action
Refusal treat as a parse failure read the category; fallback if allowed
Budget exhausted hard reject on every tenant the next rung of the ladder

Pitfalls

  • "If retrieval fails, the model still knows things"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it often produces a good-looking answer, so the feature seems to survive.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: users read answers in a sourced product as sourced, so a fabrication arrives with borrowed trust.
    ↳ Think instead: an honest "I can't reach the source" beats an unsourced answer.
  • "Fallback is free availability"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the success rate stays high and the provider blip disappears.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: a different model changes format and quality, and the incident then reads as a prompt regression.
    ↳ Think instead: no eval and no dashboard slice, no route.
  • Don't leave a degraded path unexercised.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's built for rare days, so nothing seems to need it.
    ↳ What goes wrong: the SRE book's warning applies: "the code path you never use is the code path that (often) doesn't work".
    ↳ Do instead: drive it deliberately, with a small share of traffic or a game day.
  • Don't inline a raw tool error into the prompt.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the model could explain the failure to the user.
    ↳ What goes wrong: it's weak context and an injection carrier from whoever controls that service.
    ↳ Do instead: render a typed status your own code wrote.
  • Shelf life: provider fallback is in beta and will change; "the prompt knows only what you render" won't.

Connections

Path:the gatewaydegradation and fallbackreliability engineering
  • Owned elsewhere: failure modes and resilience (LLM-Production) covers breakers and shedding.
  • Builds on the reference architecture: the renderer writes the marker.
  • Attacked by indirect injection: tool errors are untrusted text.
  • Measured by golden datasets: the failure cohort.

notes.title: Batch & Offline Prompting — Half Price for Anything No One Is Waiting For
notes.html:
References

Anthropic: batch processing · OpenAI: Batch API

TL;DR

All three major providers price asynchronous batch at half the standard rate, finished within a window of about a day. If no person is waiting for the result, it belongs in a batch. Limits per provider are in the chapter map's Landscape; the sum is cost modelling.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery request

Recall

Prompt Answer
The multiplier? × 0.5 on Anthropic, OpenAI and Gemini, as of Oct 2026.
Beyond price, why move evals to batch? OpenAI's batch limits are separate, so a large run doesn't consume live quota.
Why can a batch miss the prompt cache? Requests run concurrently, so hits are best-effort.

The idea

A nightly eval run on the live endpoint pays full price and competes with users for quota. Moved to batch, it costs half and takes longer. Evals, backfills, bulk classification and labelling all fit. The one prompt-shaped trap is caching: Anthropic reports typical hit rates of 30–98% on batches, and suggests the 1-hour lifetime, because a batch can outlast 5 minutes. Check retention too: Anthropic's batches are held for 29 days and aren't eligible for zero data retention.

Evolution

Lineage:Apr 2024 OpenAI batchOct 2024 Anthropic batch2026 flex tiers at the same price, synchronous. 🟢 Established (Oct 2026).

notes.title: Reliability Engineering — Which Failure Gets Which Response
notes.html:
References

Anthropic: API errors · OpenAI: rate limits · Anthropic: stop reasons · Google SRE: addressing cascading failures

TL;DR

Reliability here means sorting failures before responding to them. Transport errors get bounded retries, a malformed output gets one repair, a wrong-but-valid output gets no retry, and a cut-off answer needs a bigger cap or a smaller job. Two traps sit on top: retries multiply across layers, and a timeout doesn't tell you a side effect didn't happen.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery request
Flow:call with a deadlinebounded backoff

finished ─stop reason─▶ cut off or refused: no parse

parsedone repairvalidhuman or refusalpassesside effect, once

Recall

Prompt Answer
Which failures are retried as they are? Transport errors, 5xx and rate limits, bounded, under a deadline.
What bounds latency: retry count or deadline? The deadline; counts multiply across layers.
Where does idempotency live? At the side effect, not in the retry wrapper.

The idea

A service retries three times. So does the gateway. So, unnoticed, does the SDK, which on Anthropic's retries twice by default. During a brownout one user action becomes 24 provider calls, the provider gets slower, and a request budgeted at two seconds runs for minutes. Meanwhile a timed-out refund call is retried and the customer is refunded twice, because a timeout only says you didn't hear back.

Both follow from treating "retry" as one response to one kind of failure. There are at least five kinds, and they need different treatment. Sampling again can't fix a validation failure, because the model already committed to that answer. A repair can't fix a truncation, since it regenerates to the same cap.

So classify first, in code, in a fixed order: transport, then stop reason, then shape, then meaning. All of it is enforced outside the model.

The trade: one deadline, one retrying layer and a key on every side effect, at the price of more failures surfaced to the caller instead of absorbed.

How it works

Two loops, kept apart: transport retries inside the first box, at the gateway, and the single repair after the parser.

Every exit except one leads to degradation; no loop is unbounded. The repair itself is owned by parsing and repair loops.

Rule What actually happens
Retry in one layer Attempts multiply: the SRE book's example is 64 from three layers. OpenAI's guide says to disable SDK retries or account for them.
Not every 429 is a rate limit Anthropic's spend-cap 429 has no retry-after and fails until access resumes; OpenAI says not to retry quota errors.
A 200 can still fail On a stream, overloaded_error can arrive after the 200, so a started stream isn't a finished answer.
The key is derived, not generated Hash tenant, turn and action, so every attempt at one operation carries the same key.
Failed calls still count OpenAI counts them towards per-minute limits, so hammering a limit prolongs it.

Evolution

Lineage:2016 retry budgets in the SRE bookAug 2024 schema enforcement removes most shape failures2026 refusals and window limits arrive as stop reasons
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Oct 2026): the discipline is old; LLM systems add stop reasons and proposed actions.
  • Stronger-model test: no. Fewer malformed outputs shrink one loop; networks and timeouts stay. What won't change: a timeout doesn't say what happened.

Code

Break it: the belief that "3 retries" means 4 attempts, and that a retry is harmless.

sdk, gateway, app = 2, 3, 1                # retries at each layer; the SDK default is 2
attempts = (1 + sdk) * (1 + gateway) * (1 + app)
print(attempts, attempts * 10)             # provider calls, worst-case seconds at a 10 s timeout
done = set()
def refund(key, order):                    # the side effect dedupes, not the retry wrapper
    if key in done: return "skipped"
    done.add(key); return f"refunded {order}"
print([refund("turn-88:refund:4412", "4412") for _ in range(2)])
# look for: 24 attempts, 240 s, one refund
# naive belief predicts: "3 retries" means 4 attempts, and a retry is harmless

Run on Python 3.15, it prints 24 240, then ['refunded 4412', 'skipped']. The layer counts are chosen to show the product, not taken from a real system.

Measure it

  • Offline: feed canned failures to the classifier (5xx, 429 with and without retry-after, truncation, refusal, bad JSON, a rule failure), against the expected action per class.
  • In production: attempts per logical call, repair rate per version, stop reasons per version, deduped side effects. Repair rate jumping after a release is a rollback signal, not a cost line.
  • Enforced by: the deadline, one retrying layer and the key check at the side effect. Asking the model not to repeat an action is a request only.

Interview

30-second answer: I classify before responding. Transport errors get bounded retries under one deadline, in one layer. Malformed output gets one repair. Valid but wrong output isn't retried; it degrades or goes to a person. Truncation is read from the stop reason. And side effects carry a key derived from the request, because a timeout doesn't tell you the action didn't happen.

Q · Mechanism — Why is the key on the side effect rather than on the model call? Generation is safe to repeat; only money and messages aren't. A retried generation can propose the same refund twice, and a timed-out call may have succeeded. So I derive one key per logical operation and check it where refund() runs. Then any number of attempts yields one effect, whichever layer retried.

Q · Trade-off — Why not simply raise the retry count for better availability? The simpler rung is one retrying layer with a short budget, and most availability gain comes from there. More attempts multiply load on a struggling provider and spend the caller's deadline. The SRE book caps at three attempts per request and a 10% retry ratio per client. Past that, a fast failure into a degraded answer serves users better.

Compare

Failure Detect by Retry? Then
Connection, 5xx, 529 exception, status bounded, jittered evaluated fallback
429 status, retry-after if the header allows shed low priority
Cut off stop_reason, not parse with a bigger cap or smaller job restructure the output
Refusal stop_reason: "refusal" on a fallback model honest refusal
Malformed schema validation one repair structured refusal
Valid but not allowed business rule no a person, or refuse

Pitfalls

  • "Retries make the system more reliable"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: they clear transient errors, and the success rate rises.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: across layers they multiply, 24 calls in Break it, and turn a brownout into an outage. On validation failures they buy the same answer again.
    ↳ Think instead: one retrying layer, one deadline, and classify first.
  • Not the same: truncation vs a parse failure
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: cut-off JSON surfaces as a parser error.
    ↳ Difference: parsing failed because generation stopped at the cap. A repair regenerates to the same cap.
    ↳ Think instead: read the stop reason before the parser runs.
  • "A timeout means it failed"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: in the calling code it arrives as an exception, like any failure.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the work may have completed; you just didn't hear back. Retrying without a key repeats a real action.
    ↳ Think instead: unknown outcome, so dedupe at the effect.
  • Don't let a repair loop absorb a prompt defect.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: users see no errors, so the loop seems to be working.
    ↳ What goes wrong: a jump after a release hides a regression behind a higher bill and a slower tail.
    ↳ Do instead: alert on repair rate per version, and fix the prompt or the schema.
  • Shelf life: error codes, stop reasons and SDK defaults change; the order of classification doesn't.

Connections

Path:parsing and repair loopsreliability engineeringdegradation and fallbackcompliance and auditability
  • Owned elsewhere: failure modes and resilience (LLM-Production) covers breakers and backoff.
  • Costed in latency budget: each attempt spends the deadline.
  • Measured by prompt observability: repair rate per version.
  • Drilled in output length over budget.

notes.title: Compliance & Auditability — Reproduce the Inputs, Store the Output
notes.html:
References

Anthropic: model IDs and versioning · Langfuse: prompt management

TL;DR

Months later, someone asks what produced an answer. That is a logging schema decided before the request, and it can't be rebuilt afterwards. Record the inputs exactly, and store the output you served, because re-running can't reproduce it.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery request

Recall

Prompt Answer
The piece most often missing? Retrieved context as it was; documents change, so store it or its hash.
Reproducible or deterministic? Reproducible inputs only; the served output must be stored.
Does a pinned model ID freeze behaviour? Weights, yes on Anthropic; serving infrastructure can still change.

The idea

A customer disputes a decision from March. You hold the prompt, but not the chunks retrieved that day, the model ID or the output. Each record below answers one audit question.

Record Why
Template name and version what you asked
Rendered prompt, or slots plus retrieved text what the model read
Model ID, parameters who answered
Raw output, stop reason what it said
Validator verdict, action taken what you did

Anthropic, as of Oct 2026, says each model ID is a pinned snapshot, while the request router, safety classifiers and sampling logic can change around it. So even identical inputs aren't a replay. These records hold personal data, so apply PII handling.

Evolution

Lineage:prompt logs for debuggingversioned traces as an audit record. 🟡 Maturing (Oct 2026): model-ID guarantees differ by provider.

notes.title: Build vs Buy for Prompt Tooling — Decide by Who Edits the Prompts
notes.html:
References

OpenAI: migrate from prompt objects · Langfuse: prompt management

TL;DR

This looks like a tooling choice and is really an authorship question. Engineers editing prompts: keep them in the repo. Domain experts editing them: a managed store with a UI. The general form is prompts as code vs config; products are compared in registries and tooling.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchdesign time

Recall

Prompt Answer
The deciding question? Who edits the prompts.
What does buying cost you? Prompts ship outside your release process, so you add compensating controls.
What is OpenAI's position? It's moving prompts into code: v1/prompts is scheduled to shut down on 30 Nov 2026.

The idea

Repo Managed store
Fits engineers author clinicians, lawyers or support leads author
Gives PR review, evals in CI, one version system non-engineer editing, deploy by label, trace links
Must add an editing path for non-engineers protected labels, an eval gate on promotion, a client cache

Providers disagree: OpenAI's migration guide, as of Oct 2026, says prompts should "live with the product code", and Langfuse builds managed versions and labels. The simplest rung is a prompt file in the repo; buy when a named non-engineer needs to ship without a deploy.

Evolution

Lineage:Jun 2026 OpenAI de-emphasises prompt objects30 Nov 2026 scheduled shutdown. 🟡 Maturing (Oct 2026).
